subject: Slow sampling of educational measurement model (hierarchical logistic regression model)

messages.author: 7875bddbce89231c
messages.subject: Slow sampling of educational measurement model (hierarchical logistic regression model)
parts:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to implement a hierarchical logistic regression model that is somewhat related to the IRT class of models but has a few differences. For context, I am using simulated data to assess the performance of my implementation of the Reduced-DINA model (a type of Educational measurement model).  

The data are student's responses (1 = correct, 0 = incorrect) to a 30 item test that measures two latent attributes (or skills). Items 1-10 measure skill1, items 11-20 measure skill2, and items 21-30 measure skills 1 and 2. (Note: this relationship is established in a Q-matrix, but does not appear in my implementation of the model). The likelihood for an item that measures both skills (alpha1 and alpha2) is:

logit p(Y[student, item] | alpha[1], alpha[2]) = f[item] + d[item] * alpha[1] * alpha[2]

The likelihood for an item that measures only skill 1 (alpha1) is:

logit p(Y[student, item] | alpha[1]) = f[item] + d[item] * alpha[1]

Essentially f[item] acts as the baseline probability of correctly answering the question if you have not mastered all of the required skills and d[item] is the additive increase in the probability of a correct response for mastering all required skills.  In my data simulation I am tightly controlling f and d to ensure that if the student has not mastered the skills the probability of a correct response is less than 5%. If the student has mastered the skills the probability of a correct response is greater than 95%.

I've implemented the model in Stan as:

data {
  int<lower=1> I;           // number of examinees
  int<lower=1> J;           // number of items
  int<lower=1> K;           // number of skills
  int<lower=0, upper=1> y[I,J];            // correctness of examinee on item
}

parameters {
  real<lower=-20, upper=20> fHat[J];              // intercept or baseline probability
  real<lower=-20, upper=20> dHat[J];              // main effect of skill mastery
  real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha1[I];
  real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha2[I];

  real <lower=0, upper=50> a1[I];
  real <lower=0, upper=50> b1[I];
  real <lower=0, upper=50> a2[I];
  real <lower=0, upper=50> b2[I];
}

model {
  # priors for continous skill mastery
  for (i in 1:I){
    alpha1[i] ~ beta(a1[i],b1[i]);
    alpha2[i] ~ beta(a2[i],b2[i]);
  }

  a1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
  b1 ~ cauchy(0,5);

  a2 ~ cauchy(0,5);
  b2 ~ cauchy(0,5);

  # priors for RDINA parameters d and f
  dHat ~ normal(7,2);
  fHat ~ normal(-3,2);


  for (i in 1:I){
    y[i,1] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[1] + (dHat[1] * alpha1[i]));
    # items 2 - 9 omitted
    y[i,10] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[10] + (dHat[10] * alpha1[i]));
    
    y[i,11] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[11] + (dHat[11] * alpha2[i]));
    # items 12 - 19 omitted
    y[i,20] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[20] + (dHat[20] * alpha2[i]));

    y[i,21] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[21] + (dHat[21] * alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));
    # items 22 - 29 omitted
    y[i,30] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[30] + (dHat[30] * alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));
  }
}


Currently when I run the model using 1,000 students it takes about 18 hours to finish sampling (using 4 chains of n = 2000 on 4 cores). While this is obviously not terrible relative to some of the models I've read about on the list, I'd like to reduce the sampling time if at all possible as I will be conducting a large number of simulations using variations of this model.

Here are things I've explored, but been unable to resolve:
  • Fully vectorizing the response data such that y is a vector length # Items x # students (similar to the IRT model examples). The issue with this is I haven't been able to figure out how to selectively include alpha1 and alpha2 depending on whether or not the item measures those skills. My linear algebra skills are weak, so there may be an easy implementation that I am missing (perhaps a Kronecker delta function of some sort?).
  • A non-hierarchical model samples much more quickly, but I am using the hierarchical priors on alpha1 and alpha2 to help push the parameter values to 0 or 1. In JAGS I used a binomial prior on alpha1 and alpha2 but obviously STAN does not support that. 
Would anyone be kind enough to point me in the direction of some optimizations? Or any suggestions of where to look? I am new to both STAN and this type of model, so I imagine I am overlooking many things. 

Many thanks in advance!

-Dave

messages.subject: Re: Slow sampling of educational measurement model (hierarchical logistic regression model)
parts:
I can't precisely explain why, but it appears that using a bernoulii prior with the predictors specified as as 1 / (1-exp(x))  rather than a bernoulli_logit is a significant performance boost. JAGS displays similar behavior, so the bernoulli_logit transformation of the predictors must have an impact on the log density that makes it much more time consuming to sample from.

Anyone have any other ideas?

parts:
That's a different link function. inverse logit is 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) not
1 / (1 - exp(x)). In your case, if x > log(1), you get a negative value.

We don't recommend constraining your parameters to intervals unless
necessary to satisfy physical constraints --- we recommend weakly informative
or even more strongly informative priors about the scale of the expected
answers instead.

- Bob

Thanks!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling of educational measurement model (hierarchical logistic regression model)
parts:
That shouldn't be faster than

y[i, 1] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[1] + dHat[1] * (alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));

Try more runs and see if your first impressions hold up.

Also, we have an inv_logit() function specifically so users don't
have to reimplement things like this themselves.

Any time you have alpha1[i] * alpha2[i] like this it's going
to be a problem (assuming alpha1 and alpha2 are parameters). It's
not identified by itself and causes a banana-shaped posterior that's
hard to sample.

- Bob

> On May 26, 2016, at 4:15 PM, David Rackham <ddra...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Bob! It looks like my response was a typo, rather than an error in my implementation. I implemented it as:
>
> y[i, 1] ~ bernoulli(1 / (1 + exp(-fHat[1] - dHat[1] * (alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]))));
>
> What suggestions do you have for the priors? And are you referring specifically to the dHat and fHat normal priors? And to be clear, Stan does not require interval constraints on reals?
>
> Thanks!
>
>> On May 26, 2016, at 1:01 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> That's a different link function. inverse logit is 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) not
>> 1 / (1 - exp(x)). In your case, if x > log(1), you get a negative value.
>>
>> We don't recommend constraining your parameters to intervals unless
>> necessary to satisfy physical constraints --- we recommend weakly informative
>> or even more strongly informative priors about the scale of the expected
>> answers instead.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>> On May 26, 2016, at 12:13 PM, David Rackham <ddra...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> I can't precisely explain why, but it appears that using a bernoulii prior with the predictors specified as as 1 / (1-exp(x)) rather than a bernoulli_logit is a significant performance boost. JAGS displays similar behavior, so the bernoulli_logit transformation of the predictors must have an impact on the log density that makes it much more time consuming to sample from.
>>>
>>> Anyone have any other ideas?
>>>
>>> On Friday, May 20, 2016 at 2:30:50 PM UTC-6, David Rackham wrote:
>>> Hi everyone,
>>>
>>> I am trying to implement a hierarchical logistic regression model that is somewhat related to the IRT class of models but has a few differences. For context, I am using simulated data to assess the performance of my implementation of the Reduced-DINA model (a type of Educational measurement model).
>>>
>>> The data are student's responses (1 = correct, 0 = incorrect) to a 30 item test that measures two latent attributes (or skills). Items 1-10 measure skill1, items 11-20 measure skill2, and items 21-30 measure skills 1 and 2. (Note: this relationship is established in a Q-matrix, but does not appear in my implementation of the model). The likelihood for an item that measures both skills (alpha1 and alpha2) is:
>>>
>>> logit p(Y[student, item] | alpha[1], alpha[2]) = f[item] + d[item] * alpha[1] * alpha[2]
>>>
>>> The likelihood for an item that measures only skill 1 (alpha1) is:
>>>
>>> logit p(Y[student, item] | alpha[1]) = f[item] + d[item] * alpha[1]
>>>
>>> Essentially f[item] acts as the baseline probability of correctly answering the question if you have not mastered all of the required skills and d[item] is the additive increase in the probability of a correct response for mastering all required skills. In my data simulation I am tightly controlling f and d to ensure that if the student has not mastered the skills the probability of a correct response is less than 5%. If the student has mastered the skills the probability of a correct response is greater than 95%.
>>>
>>> I've implemented the model in Stan as:
>>>
>>> data {
>>> int<lower=1> I; // number of examinees
>>> int<lower=1> J; // number of items
>>> int<lower=1> K; // number of skills
>>> int<lower=0, upper=1> y[I,J]; // correctness of examinee on item
>>> }
>>>
>>> parameters {
>>> real<lower=-20, upper=20> fHat[J]; // intercept or baseline probability
>>> real<lower=-20, upper=20> dHat[J]; // main effect of skill mastery
>>> real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha1[I];
>>> real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha2[I];
>>>
>>> real <lower=0, upper=50> a1[I];
>>> real <lower=0, upper=50> b1[I];
>>> real <lower=0, upper=50> a2[I];
>>> real <lower=0, upper=50> b2[I];
>>> }
>>>
>>> model {
>>> # priors for continous skill mastery
>>> for (i in 1:I){
>>> alpha1[i] ~ beta(a1[i],b1[i]);
>>> alpha2[i] ~ beta(a2[i],b2[i]);
>>> }
>>>
>>> a1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>>> b1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>>>
>>> a2 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>>> b2 ~ cauchy(0,5);
>>>
>>> # priors for RDINA parameters d and f
>>> dHat ~ normal(7,2);
>>> fHat ~ normal(-3,2);
>>>
>>>
>>> for (i in 1:I){
>>> y[i,1] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[1] + (dHat[1] * alpha1[i]));
>>> # items 2 - 9 omitted
>>> y[i,10] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[10] + (dHat[10] * alpha1[i]));
>>>
>>> y[i,11] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[11] + (dHat[11] * alpha2[i]));
>>> # items 12 - 19 omitted
>>> y[i,20] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[20] + (dHat[20] * alpha2[i]));
>>>
>>> y[i,21] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[21] + (dHat[21] * alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));
>>> # items 22 - 29 omitted
>>> y[i,30] ~ bernoulli_logit(fHat[30] + (dHat[30] * alpha1[i] * alpha2[i]));
>>> }
>>> }
>>>
>>>
>>> Currently when I run the model using 1,000 students it takes about 18 hours to finish sampling (using 4 chains of n = 2000 on 4 cores). While this is obviously not terrible relative to some of the models I've read about on the list, I'd like to reduce the sampling time if at all possible as I will be conducting a large number of simulations using variations of this model.
>>>
>>> Here are things I've explored, but been unable to resolve:
>>> • Fully vectorizing the response data such that y is a vector length # Items x # students (similar to the IRT model examples). The issue with this is I haven't been able to figure out how to selectively include alpha1 and alpha2 depending on whether or not the item measures those skills. My linear algebra skills are weak, so there may be an easy implementation that I am missing (perhaps a Kronecker delta function of some sort?).
>>> • A non-hierarchical model samples much more quickly, but I am using the hierarchical priors on alpha1 and alpha2 to help push the parameter values to 0 or 1. In JAGS I used a binomial prior on alpha1 and alpha2 but obviously STAN does not support that.
>>> Would anyone be kind enough to point me in the direction of some optimizations? Or any suggestions of where to look? I am new to both STAN and this type of model, so I imagine I am overlooking many things.
>>>
>>> Many thanks in advance!
>>>
>>> -Dave
